threads.body: Apache HttpAsyncClient may derive the request Content-Type from the entity (e.g., StringEntity defaulting to text/plain; charset=UTF-8). Setting a separate header risks sending a conflicting or unexpected Content-Type, which can break the shared HTTP contract expectations. Prefer constructing the entity with an explicit JSON content type that matches HttpContract.CONTENT_TYPE (and avoid duplicating/conflicting Content-Type headers).

replies.body:
Addressed in c790ab857858f24fe2570d3ba7868554cba26f5a.

Analysis: Both Apache clients should derive the request Content-Type from one entity. Creating that entity from `HttpContract.CONTENT_TYPE` avoids a conflicting standalone header and avoids the charset parameter in `ContentType.APPLICATION_JSON`.

Upsides: Both clients emit the exact contract content type from one source and encode request bodies as UTF-8.

Downsides: Each request body requires an intermediate byte array.

threads.body: ContentType.APPLICATION_JSON commonly includes a charset parameter (e.g., application/json; charset=UTF-8). If the shared contract expects the Content-Type to match HttpContract.CONTENT_TYPE exactly, this can cause conformance mismatches. Consider using a ContentType parsed/created directly from HttpContract.CONTENT_TYPE (and set the Content-Type in one place) so the emitted header matches the contract precisely.

threads.body: This uses `Future#get()` without a timeout, which can hang indefinitely if the mock server is unreachable or a request stalls (making CI runs flaky). Use a bounded wait (e.g., `.get(HttpClientWorkload.REQUEST_TIMEOUT.toMillis(), TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)`) so every request is guaranteed to complete or fail within the scenario timeout.

replies.body:
Addressed in 47f243b03da8858e8e2b4867c255d6d42338cdcd.

Analysis: The shared request timeout should cover each explicit future wait, both HttpURLConnection network phases, and Vert.x shutdown. The same change also bounds the sibling Apache HttpAsyncClient future.

Upsides: These clients now use one timeout for requests and shutdown, and a stalled operation fails within 30 seconds.

Downsides: A network operation or shutdown that legitimately needs more than 30 seconds now fails.

threads.body:
One catch-all context collapses all six exchanges into one route: the agent reads `http.route` from `exchange.getHttpContext().getPath()`. Running the package on this branch:

```
GET /    route=/   url.path=/health
GET /    route=/   url.path=/users/123
POST /   route=/   url.path=/items
GET /    route=/   url.path=/status/404
```

Every other route-emitting server here keeps them apart - servlet and tomcat report `/users/*`, helidon and restlet `/users/{userId}` - so this is the one package where the contract's parameterized-route case and the span name built from it aren't measured.

One context per prefix fixes it; I ran it and got `/health`, `/users/`, `/items`, `/status/`, with `data.json` unchanged, since coverage records attribute keys rather than values.

```java
server.createContext("/health", JavaHttpServerServerScenario::answer);
server.createContext("/users/", JavaHttpServerServerScenario::answer);
server.createContext("/items", JavaHttpServerServerScenario::answer);
server.createContext("/status/", JavaHttpServerServerScenario::answer);
```

`REQUEST_TIMEOUT` is not applied here, and an `HttpRequest` with no timeout waits forever, so a stalled mock server hangs the run until the job times out instead of failing.

```java
HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI.create(url)).timeout(HttpClientWorkload.REQUEST_TIMEOUT)
```

Same gap in `apache-httpclient` (`ConnectionConfig` leaves the socket timeout unset and `RequestConfig.responseTimeout` is null) and `jodd-http` (`timeout` defaults to -1, so `SO_TIMEOUT` 0). OkHttp, Ratpack and Jetty already bound it by default; the four that use the constant fail with a clear error. These three don't.
there does not seem to be a launcher / conformace.yaml for this one
Same as the WebFlux one: no launcher and no `server/conformance.yaml` reference this class.
